{{Short description|Algebraic structure}}
In mathematics, a '''J-structure''' is an [[algebraic structure]] over a [[field (algebra)|field]] related to a [[Jordan algebra]].  The concept was introduced by {{harvtxt|Springer|1973}} to develop a theory of Jordan algebras using [[linear algebraic group]]s and axioms taking the Jordan inversion as basic operation and [[Hua's identity]] as a basic relation.  There is a classification of simple structures deriving from the classification of [[semisimple algebraic group]]s.  Over fields of [[characteristic of a field|characteristic]] not equal to 2, the theory of J-structures is essentially the same as that of Jordan algebras.

==Definition==
Let ''V'' be a [[finite-dimensional vector space]] over a field ''K'' and ''j'' a [[rational map]] from ''V'' to itself, expressible in the form ''n''/''N'' with ''n'' a [[polynomial map]] from ''V'' to itself and ''N'' a polynomial in ''K''[''V''].  Let ''H'' be the subset of GL(''V'') × GL(''V'') containing the pairs (''g'',''h'') such that ''g''∘''j'' = ''j''∘''h'': it is a closed [[subgroup]] of the product and the projection onto the first factor, the set of ''g'' which occur, is the ''structure group'' of ''j'', denoted ''G'''(''j'').

A ''J-structure'' is a triple (''V'',''j'',''e'') where ''V'' is a vector space over ''K'', ''j'' is a [[birational map]] from ''V'' to itself and ''e'' is a non-zero element of ''V'' satisfying the following conditions.<ref name=Spr10>Springer (1973) p.10</ref>
* ''j'' is a homogeneous birational [[Involution (mathematics)|involution]] of degree −1
* ''j'' is regular at ''e'' and ''j''(''e'') = ''e''
* if ''j'' is regular at ''x'', ''e'' + ''x'' and ''e'' + ''j''(''x'') then
:<math> j(e+x) + j(e+j(x)) = e </math>
* the orbit ''G'' ''e'' of ''e'' under the structure group ''G'' = ''G''(''j'') is a [[Zariski open]] subset of ''V''.

The ''norm'' associated to a J-structure (''V'',''j'',''e'') is the numerator ''N'' of ''j'', normalised so that ''N''(''e'') = 1.  The ''degree'' of the J-structure is the degree of ''N'' as a homogeneous polynomial map.<ref name=Spr11>Springer (1973) p.11</ref>

The ''quadratic map'' of the structure is a map ''P'' from ''V'' to End(''V'') defined in terms of the [[Differential (mathematics)#Algebraic geometry|differential]] d''j'' at an invertible ''x''.<ref name=Spr16>Springer (1973) p.16</ref>  We put
:<math>P(x) = - (d j)_x^{-1} . </math>

The quadratic map turns out to be a quadratic polynomial map on ''V''.

The subgroup of the structure group ''G'' generated by the invertible quadratic maps is the ''inner structure group'' of the J-structure.  It is a closed connected normal subgroup.<ref name=Spr18>Springer (1973) p.18</ref>

==J-structures from quadratic forms==
Let ''K'' have [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] not equal to 2. Let ''Q'' be a [[quadratic form]] on the vector space ''V'' over ''K'' with associated [[bilinear form]] ''Q''(''x'',''y'') = ''Q''(''x''+''y'') − ''Q''(''x'') − ''Q''(''y'') and distinguished element ''e'' such that ''Q''(''e'',.) is not trivial.  We define a reflection map ''x''<sup>*</sup> by

:<math> x^* = Q(x,e)e - x </math>

and an inversion map ''j'' by

:<math> j(x) = Q(x)^{-1} x^* . </math>

Then (''V'',''j'',''e'') is a J-structure.

===Example===
Let ''Q'' be the usual sum of squares quadratic function on ''K''<sup>''r''</sup> for fixed integer ''r'', equipped with the [[standard basis]] ''e''<sup>1</sup>,...,''e''<sup>''r''</sup>.  Then (''K''<sup>''r''</sup>, ''Q'', ''e''<sup>''r''</sup>) is a J-structure of degree 2.  It is denoted O<sub>2</sub>.<ref name=Spr33>Springer (1973) p.33</ref>

==Link with Jordan algebras==
In [[characteristic of a field|characteristic]] not equal to 2, which we assume in this section, the theory of J-structures is essentially the same as that of Jordan algebras.

Let ''A'' be a finite-dimensional commutative [[non-associative algebra]] over ''K'' with identity ''e''.   Let ''L''(''x'') denote multiplication on the left by ''x''.  There is a unique birational map ''i'' on ''A'' such that ''i''(''x'').''x'' = ''e'' if ''i'' is regular on ''x'': it is homogeneous of degree −1 and an involution with ''i''(''e'') = ''e''.  It may be defined by ''i''(''x'') = ''L''(''x'')<sup>−1</sup>.''e''.  We call ''i'' the ''inversion'' on ''A''.<ref name=Spr66>Springer (1973) p.66</ref>

A Jordan algebra is defined by the identity<ref name=Sch91>Schafer (1995) p.91</ref><ref name=Oku13>Okubo (2005) p.13</ref>

:<math> x(x^2 y) = x^2 (x y) . </math>

An alternative characterisation is that for all invertible ''x'' we have

:<math> x^{-1}(x y) = x (x^{-1} y) . </math>

If ''A'' is a Jordan algebra, then (''A'',''i'',''e'') is a J-structure.  If (''V'',''j'',''e'') is a J-structure, then there exists a unique Jordan algebra structure on ''V'' with identity ''e'' with inversion ''j''.

==Link with quadratic Jordan algebras==
In general characteristic, which we assume in this section, J-structures are related to [[quadratic Jordan algebra]]s.  We take a quadratic Jordan algebra to be a finite dimensional vector space ''V'' with a quadratic map ''Q'' from ''V'' to End(''V'') and a distinguished element ''e''.  We let ''Q'' also denote the bilinear map ''Q''(''x'',''y'') = ''Q''(''x''+''y'') − ''Q''(''x'') − ''Q''(''y'').  The properties of a quadratic Jordan algebra will be<ref name=Spr72>Springer (1973) p.72</ref><ref name=McC83>McCrimmon (2004) p.83</ref>
* ''Q''(''e'') = id<sub>''V''</sub>, ''Q''(''x'',''e'')''y'' = ''Q''(''x'',''y'')''e''
* ''Q''(''Q''(''x'')''y'') = ''Q''(''x'')''Q''(''y'')''Q''(''x'')
* ''Q''(''x'')''Q''(''y'',''z'')''x'' = ''Q''(''Q''(''x'')''y'',''x'')''z''

We call ''Q''(''x'')''e'' the ''square'' of ''x''.  If the squaring is [[dominant morphism|dominant]] (has [[Zariski dense]] image) then the algebra is termed ''separable''.<ref name=Spr74>Springer (1973) p.74</ref>

There is a unique birational involution ''i'' such that ''Q''(''x'')''i'' ''x'' = ''x'' if ''Q'' is regular at ''x''.  As before, ''i'' is the ''inversion'', definable by ''i''(''x'') = ''Q''(''x'')<sup>−1</sup> ''x''.

If (''V'',''j'',''e'') is a J-structure, with quadratic map ''Q'' then (''V'',''Q'',''e'') is a quadratic Jordan algebra.  In the opposite direction, if (''V'',''Q'',''e'') is a separable quadratic Jordan algebra with inversion ''i'', then (''V'',''i'',''e'') is a J-structure.<ref name=Spr76>Springer (1973) p.76</ref>

===H-structure===
McCrimmon proposed a notion of ''H-structure'' by dropping the density axiom and strengthening the third (a form of Hua's identity) to hold in all [[Mutation (algebra)|isotopes]].  The resulting structure is categorically equivalent to a quadratic Jordan algebra.<ref name=McC1977>McCrimmon (1977)</ref><ref name=McC1978>McCrimmon (1978)</ref>

==Peirce decomposition==
A J-structure has a [[Peirce decomposition]] into subspaces determined by idempotent elements.<ref name=Spr90>Springer (1973) p.90</ref>  Let ''a'' be an idempotent of the J-structure (''V'',''j'',''e''), that is, ''a''<sup>2</sup> = ''a''.  Let ''Q'' be the quadratic map.  Define

:<math>\phi_a(t,u) = Q(ta + u(e-a)) . </math>

This is invertible for non-zero ''t'',''u'' in ''K'' and so φ defines a morphism from the [[algebraic torus]] GL<sub>1</sub> × GL<sub>1</sub> to the inner structure group ''G''<sub>1</sub>.  There are subspaces

:<math> V_a = \left\lbrace{ x \in V : \phi_a(t,u) x = t^2 x }\right\rbrace </math>
:<math> V'_a = \left\lbrace{ x \in V : \phi_a(t,u) x = tu x }\right\rbrace </math>
:<math> V_{e-a} = \left\lbrace{ x \in V : \phi_a(t,u) x = u^2 x }\right\rbrace </math>

and these form a [[direct sum]] decomposition of ''V''.  This is the Peirce decomposition for the idempotent ''a''.<ref name=Spr92>Springer (1973) p.92</ref>

==Generalisations==
If we drop the condition on the distinguished element ''e'', we obtain "J-structures without identity".<ref name=Spr21>Springer (1973) p.21</ref>  These are related to [[isotope (Jordan algebra)|isotope]]s of Jordan algebras.<ref name=Spr22>Springer (1973) p.22</ref>
